questions.scenario: A Lambda function runs 200 million times per month, completing in 20 ms at 256 MB. The team wants to reduce cost. Which analysis is correct?
options: Increase memory to reduce duration and therefore cost
At 20 ms the function is likely dominated by the per-request charge, so reducing invocation count through batching would save more than memory tuning
Add provisioned concurrency
Increase the timeout
questions.explain: Lambda bills a per-request charge plus GB-seconds. At only 20 ms the compute component is tiny, so the request charge dominates at 200 million invocations and memory tuning yields little. Batching many items per invocation cuts the request count directly. Provisioned concurrency adds idle cost, and timeout is only a ceiling.

questions.scenario: A DynamoDB table serves 1,000 reads per second of 2 KB items, all of which could tolerate slightly stale data. The team uses strongly consistent reads. What is the cost impact of switching to eventually consistent?
options: No change
Read capacity consumption halves, because eventually consistent reads cost half an RCU per 4 KB
Consumption doubles
Consumption quadruples
questions.explain: A 2 KB item rounds up to one 4 KB unit, costing 1 RCU strongly consistent or 0.5 RCU eventually consistent. Switching therefore halves read capacity consumption and cost. Because the workload tolerates staleness, this is free money — one of the simplest DynamoDB optimisations.

questions.scenario: An application stores 50 TB of logs in S3 Standard, of which only the last 30 days are ever queried. What is the MOST cost-effective change that preserves access?
options: Delete everything older than 30 days
A lifecycle policy transitioning objects to Standard-IA then Glacier classes by age
Move everything to Glacier Deep Archive immediately
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
questions.explain: Lifecycle transitions keep recent data instantly queryable in Standard while ageing the rest into progressively cheaper classes, preserving access at a fraction of the cost. Deleting loses the data, moving everything to Deep Archive makes the queried 30 days slow and expensive to retrieve, and Transfer Acceleration affects upload speed rather than storage cost.

questions.scenario: An API receives 100 requests per second, of which 95 percent are identical GET requests for data that changes every 10 minutes. Which change reduces backend cost MOST?
options: Enable API Gateway stage caching with a TTL near 10 minutes
Increase Lambda memory
Add a second Lambda function
Switch to on-demand DynamoDB
questions.explain: Caching identical GETs for close to the data's change interval eliminates roughly 95 percent of backend invocations and downstream reads, which is by far the largest lever here. Memory changes per-invocation cost rather than invocation count, an extra function adds cost, and capacity mode does not reduce the number of requests.

questions.scenario: Which TWO changes reduce DynamoDB cost for a write-heavy workload?
options: Remove unused global secondary indexes
Batch writes with BatchWriteItem to reduce request overhead
Enable strongly consistent reads
Increase item size by denormalising heavily
Add more local secondary indexes
questions.explain: Every write must also update each GSI, so removing unused indexes cuts write capacity consumption proportionally, and batching reduces per-request overhead. Read consistency does not affect writes, larger items consume more WCU per write, and additional indexes increase write cost rather than reducing it.

questions.scenario: A team must choose between provisioned and on-demand DynamoDB capacity for a table with steady, predictable traffic at 80 percent utilisation. Which is MORE cost-effective and why?
options: On-demand, because it requires no planning
Provisioned, because steady predictable traffic at high utilisation is significantly cheaper per request
On-demand, because it is always cheaper
They cost the same
questions.explain: On-demand costs substantially more per request but eliminates planning and idle waste, which suits spiky or unpredictable workloads. Steady traffic at high utilisation is exactly the case where provisioned capacity — optionally with auto scaling or reserved capacity — is far cheaper.

questions.scenario: A Lambda function processes SQS messages one at a time with a batch size of 1, handling 10 million messages per month. What is the simplest cost optimisation?
options: Increase the batch size so each invocation processes multiple messages
Increase memory
Enable provisioned concurrency
Switch to a FIFO queue
questions.explain: A batch size of 1 means one invocation per message, so the per-request charge is paid ten million times. Raising the batch size processes many messages per invocation, cutting invocation count and cost dramatically. Memory affects duration cost, provisioned concurrency adds charges, and FIFO queues are more expensive per request.

questions.scenario: An application must store 1 KB of state per user for 10 million users, read occasionally and written rarely. Which storage is MOST cost-effective?
options: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis
Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity
Amazon S3 with one object per user
Amazon RDS with a row per user
questions.explain: DynamoDB stores 10 GB cheaply and charges per request, which suits infrequent access with no idle cost. ElastiCache would require holding all 10 GB in memory continuously, which is far more expensive for rarely-read data. Ten million tiny S3 objects incur high per-request costs, and RDS means paying for a running instance.

questions.scenario: A team must decide between Kinesis Data Streams provisioned mode and on-demand mode for a stream with unpredictable traffic between 1 and 20 MB per second. Which is BEST?
options: Provisioned with 20 shards permanently
On-demand, which scales automatically and avoids paying for peak capacity during quiet periods
Provisioned with 1 shard
Replace Kinesis with SQS
questions.explain: On-demand scales shard capacity automatically and bills for throughput used, which fits a twentyfold swing in traffic. Provisioning 20 shards permanently pays for peak all the time, one shard throttles badly at peak, and SQS does not provide ordering, replay or multiple independent consumers.

questions.scenario: An application makes 1 million KMS Decrypt calls per day to decrypt the same data key repeatedly. What is the MOST effective optimisation?
options: Cache the decrypted data key in memory with a bounded lifetime and reuse it
Switch to a cheaper KMS key type
Call kms:Encrypt instead
Disable encryption
questions.explain: KMS bills per API call, so caching a decrypted data key within bounded limits — as the AWS Encryption SDK does — collapses a million calls into a handful while keeping the plaintext key only in memory. Key type does not change per-call pricing, Encrypt is a different operation, and disabling encryption breaks the security requirement.

questions.scenario: A Lambda function is attached to a VPC and calls S3 100 million times per month through a NAT gateway. What is the MOST significant cost saving available?
options: Replace the NAT gateway path with a gateway VPC endpoint for S3, which has no hourly or data-processing charge
Increase Lambda memory
Reduce the function timeout
Move to a larger subnet
questions.explain: NAT gateways charge both hourly and per gigabyte processed, so routing high-volume S3 traffic through one is expensive. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 carries no additional charge and keeps traffic on the AWS network. Memory, timeout and subnet sizing do not affect data-processing charges.

questions.scenario: An application performs a DynamoDB Scan every minute over a 10 GB table to find items with a specific status. What is the cost problem and the correct fix?
options: Scans consume capacity for the entire table on every run; use a sparse GSI on the status attribute
Scans are free; no change needed
Increase read capacity
Enable DAX to cache the scan
questions.explain: Each Scan reads all 10 GB regardless of how few items match, so running it every minute is enormously wasteful. A sparse GSI containing only items with that status turns it into a tiny Query. Extra capacity pays more for the same waste, and DAX caches item reads rather than making full scans cheap.

questions.scenario: A team must choose between Fargate and Lambda for a workload running 200 times per day for 4 minutes each. Which is likely cheaper and why?
options: Fargate, because it has no per-request charge
Lambda, because it bills only for the 4 minutes of execution with no task startup overhead or minimum billing period
They cost identically
Neither can run this workload
questions.explain: Four minutes fits within Lambda's 15-minute limit, and Lambda bills purely for execution time with no minimum duration or provisioning overhead. Fargate adds task startup time and bills a minimum period per task, making it more expensive for short, infrequent runs — its advantage appears with longer or continuous workloads.

questions.scenario: An application uses SNS to notify 5 SQS queues, but 4 of the consumers discard 90 percent of messages after inspecting them. What change reduces cost MOST?
options: Apply subscription filter policies so each queue receives only relevant messages
Increase consumer concurrency
Switch to a single queue
Increase SQS retention
questions.explain: Filtering at SNS avoids paying for delivery, storage and consumption of messages that will be discarded anyway, cutting SQS request and Lambda invocation costs across four consumers. More concurrency processes waste faster, a single queue breaks the fan-out, and longer retention has no effect on volume.

questions.scenario: Which approach reduces Lambda cost for a function that spends 90 percent of its duration waiting for a downstream HTTP response?
options: Batch multiple items per invocation so the wait is amortised, or restructure so waiting happens outside billed compute
Increase memory to the maximum
Reduce the timeout
Add more layers
questions.explain: Because Lambda bills wall-clock time, waiting is billed the same as computing. Batching amortises a single wait across many items, and patterns such as Step Functions callbacks move the wait outside billed compute entirely. Maximum memory raises the per-millisecond price without shortening a remote call.

questions.scenario: A team stores 100 million small objects in S3 and lists them frequently to find recent uploads. Listing is slow and costly. What is the BEST improvement?
options: Maintain an index of object keys and metadata in DynamoDB and query that instead of listing S3
Enable S3 Versioning
Increase the S3 request rate limit
Use S3 Standard-IA
questions.explain: S3 LIST operations paginate 1,000 keys at a time and are not designed as a query interface, so at 100 million objects they are slow and expensive. Keeping searchable metadata in DynamoDB turns discovery into an indexed query. Versioning adds objects, request limits scale automatically, and storage class does not affect listing cost.

questions.scenario: An application writes 5 KB items to DynamoDB 1,000 times per second. How much write capacity is required for the base table alone?
options: 5,000 WCU, because a 5 KB item consumes 5 WCU
500 WCU
questions.explain: One WCU covers up to 1 KB per write with rounding up, so a 5 KB item costs 5 WCU and 1,000 writes per second requires 5,000 WCU on the base table — plus the same again for each GSI. Forgetting to multiply by item size is a common cause of unexpected throttling.

questions.scenario: Which design reduces cost for an application that must respond within 50 ms to reads of data that changes once per day?
options: Cache aggressively with a long TTL, since the data is nearly static
Query the database on every request with strongly consistent reads
Add more database capacity
Use a Scan with a filter
questions.explain: Data that changes daily can be cached for hours, so nearly every read is served from cache at minimal cost and well within the latency budget. Querying on every request pays repeatedly for the same answer, strongly consistent reads double that cost, and scanning is the most expensive option of all.

questions.scenario: A team runs a Step Functions Standard workflow 5 million times per month with 20 states each. Costs are unexpectedly high. What is the MOST likely explanation and fix?
options: Standard workflows bill per state transition, so 100 million transitions is expensive; use Express workflows for high-volume short executions
Step Functions bills per hour; reduce the duration
The Lambda functions are the cost; reduce their memory
State machines bill per definition; simplify the template
questions.explain: Standard workflows charge per state transition, so 5 million executions with 20 states each generates 100 million billed transitions. Express workflows bill by request count and duration instead, which is dramatically cheaper for high-volume executions completing within five minutes.

questions.scenario: An application must choose between storing 500 GB of infrequently accessed data in DynamoDB or S3. Which is MORE cost-effective for storage alone?
options: DynamoDB, because it is optimised for large data
S3, because its per-gigabyte storage cost is far lower than DynamoDB's
They cost the same per gigabyte
Neither can store 500 GB
questions.explain: DynamoDB storage is priced for low-latency indexed access and costs far more per gigabyte than S3, which is designed for bulk object storage. The common pattern keeps large payloads in S3 with small indexed pointers in DynamoDB, combining cheap storage with fast lookup.

questions.scenario: Which change is MOST likely to reduce the cost of an application making many small writes to S3?
options: Buffer records and write fewer, larger objects
Enable versioning
Switch to Glacier immediately
Enable Transfer Acceleration
questions.explain: S3 charges per PUT request, so many tiny objects incur high request costs and add listing overhead. Buffering into fewer larger objects — the approach Firehose automates — cuts request charges substantially. Versioning multiplies stored objects, Glacier adds retrieval cost and delay for active data, and Transfer Acceleration adds a premium.

questions.scenario: An organisation has 300 microservices, each needing a database credential. Cost review shows Secrets Manager charges are significant. Which change reduces cost while preserving security?
options: Move non-rotating configuration to Parameter Store and keep only genuinely rotating secrets in Secrets Manager
Hard-code the credentials
Store all credentials in one shared secret
Disable encryption
questions.explain: Secrets Manager charges per secret per month, so its cost is justified only where automatic rotation is genuinely required; everything else belongs in Parameter Store standard parameters, which are free and still support KMS encryption. Hard-coding and disabling encryption trade security for cost, and one shared secret destroys isolation between services.

questions.scenario: A security review requires that a Lambda function can read exactly one S3 prefix and nothing else. Which policy resource is correct?
options: arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/monthly/* for object actions, plus the bucket ARN with a prefix condition for ListBucket
arn:aws:s3:::* for all actions
arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket for all actions
* for all resources
questions.explain: Object actions require an object ARN including the prefix, while ListBucket is a bucket-level action needing the bucket ARN, typically with an s3:prefix condition to limit what can be listed. Using a wildcard across all buckets or granting the whole bucket exceeds the requirement and violates least privilege.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST cost-effective way to satisfy a requirement that all data be encrypted at rest in S3 with an audit trail of key usage?
options: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, using S3 Bucket Keys to reduce KMS request costs
SSE-S3 only
Client-side encryption with a custom key store
No encryption with a restrictive bucket policy
questions.explain: SSE-KMS provides the CloudTrail audit trail and key control the requirement demands, and S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS request charges substantially by decreasing calls to KMS. SSE-S3 offers no per-use audit trail, a custom key store adds significant cost and operational burden, and a bucket policy provides no encryption at all.

questions.scenario: An application must allow users to reset their own passwords without administrator involvement. Which Cognito feature provides this?
options: User pool self-service password reset with a verified email or phone
An identity pool unauthenticated role
IAM password policy
AWS Directory Service
questions.explain: Cognito user pools include self-service password reset flows using a verification code sent to a verified email or phone number, requiring no administrator action. Identity pools issue AWS credentials rather than managing passwords, IAM password policies apply to IAM users, and Directory Service manages Active Directory.

questions.scenario: Which TWO practices reduce the risk of over-privileged IAM roles accumulating over time?
options: Review IAM Access Analyzer findings and last-accessed data to remove unused permissions
Generate policies from CloudTrail activity rather than starting with wildcards
Grant AdministratorAccess and monitor CloudTrail
Create one shared role for all services
Disable IAM auditing to reduce noise
questions.explain: Access Analyzer and service last-accessed data identify permissions that are never used and can safely be removed, and generating policies from observed CloudTrail activity produces least-privilege policies grounded in real behaviour. Broad access with monitoring detects misuse without preventing it, shared roles blur boundaries, and disabling auditing removes the evidence needed to tighten policies.

questions.scenario: A developer must ensure an application can read a KMS-encrypted SQS queue and an encrypted S3 bucket using different keys. What is required?
options: kms:Decrypt on both key ARNs, plus the relevant SQS and S3 permissions
kms:Decrypt on one key only
No KMS permissions, since the services decrypt automatically
kms:CreateKey
questions.explain: Each KMS key requires its own permission grant, so the role needs kms:Decrypt on both key ARNs alongside the service-level SQS and S3 permissions. Services do not decrypt on a caller's behalf without the caller holding key permissions, and CreateKey is unrelated to using existing keys.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST limits the damage if an application's IAM role credentials are exfiltrated?
options: Least-privilege permissions plus conditions restricting use to expected sources such as a VPC endpoint
A longer session duration
Storing credentials in environment variables
Granting broad permissions but enabling CloudTrail
questions.explain: Narrow permissions limit what stolen credentials can do, and conditions such as aws:SourceVpce mean they are unusable from outside the expected network path. Longer sessions extend the window of misuse, environment variables are readable by the same compromised process, and CloudTrail records the damage without preventing it.

questions.scenario: An API must accept requests only from an allowlisted set of partner IP ranges, with the check applied before any compute is invoked. What should be used?
options: An API Gateway resource policy with an aws:SourceIp condition
A check inside the Lambda function
A security group on the API
A Cognito authorizer
questions.explain: A resource policy is evaluated by API Gateway before the integration runs, so non-allowlisted requests are rejected without invoking any compute — saving cost and reducing attack surface. Checking inside the function means paying for every rejected request, API Gateway is a managed service without security groups, and Cognito authenticates users rather than filtering networks.

questions.scenario: Which statement about S3 Bucket Keys is correct?
options: They reduce KMS request costs by using a bucket-level key to generate data keys for many objects
They replace KMS entirely
They disable encryption
They require client-side encryption
questions.explain: S3 Bucket Keys reduce the number of KMS API calls by deriving a short-lived bucket-level key used across many object operations, cutting SSE-KMS request costs substantially for high-volume workloads while retaining KMS key control. Encryption remains enabled and server-side throughout.

questions.scenario: A developer must decide where to validate a JWT for an API with 50 endpoints. What is the BEST approach?
options: A single authorizer at the API Gateway level, with results cached
Duplicate validation code in each of the 50 backend functions
Validation in the client only
No validation, relying on network controls
questions.explain: An authorizer validates once at the edge for every endpoint and caches the resulting policy, so unauthorised requests never reach compute and the logic exists in one place. Duplicating validation across 50 functions guarantees inconsistency, client-side validation is trivially bypassed, and network controls do not authenticate users.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct interpretation of an S3 bucket policy that denies all actions unless aws:SecureTransport is true?
options: All requests must use HTTPS; plain HTTP requests are rejected
All requests must come from a VPC
All requests must be authenticated with MFA
All objects must be encrypted
questions.explain: aws:SecureTransport is true only when a request arrives over TLS, so denying when it is false enforces HTTPS and protects data in transit. It says nothing about network origin, MFA or object encryption, which are governed by other conditions entirely.

questions.scenario: An application must prevent a specific IAM role from ever deleting objects in a bucket, even if a future policy grants it. Which control is MOST durable?
options: An explicit Deny for s3:DeleteObject in the bucket policy or a service control policy
Removing the delete permission from the role's current policy
Enabling versioning
Adding a tag
questions.explain: An explicit Deny overrides every present and future Allow, so it survives well-intentioned policy changes. Simply omitting the permission today leaves it available for someone to grant tomorrow. Versioning allows recovery after deletion rather than preventing it, and an unreferenced tag enforces nothing.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST secures an internal API called only by other services inside a VPC?
options: A private API Gateway endpoint with a resource policy restricting access to the VPC endpoint, plus IAM authorisation
A public endpoint with an API key
A public endpoint with IP allowlisting only
No authentication, relying on obscurity
questions.explain: Combining a private endpoint with a resource policy and IAM authorisation gives both network isolation and authenticated authorisation — defence in depth for service-to-service traffic. API keys do not authenticate, IP allowlists alone leave the endpoint publicly reachable, and obscurity is not a control.

questions.scenario: A developer must ensure that credentials used by a CI/CD pipeline expire automatically. Which approach achieves this?
options: Use OIDC federation so the pipeline exchanges a signed token for temporary AWS credentials
Store long-lived access keys in the pipeline settings
Rotate access keys manually every year
Use root credentials
questions.explain: OIDC federation lets the CI provider present a signed identity token that AWS exchanges for short-lived credentials, so no long-lived secret exists in the pipeline at all. Stored access keys persist until someone rotates them, annual rotation leaves a year-long exposure window, and root credentials must never be used.

questions.scenario: Which practice correctly protects PII in an application's DynamoDB table?
options: Encrypt sensitive attributes client-side before writing, and restrict access with least-privilege IAM policies
Rely solely on DynamoDB's default encryption at rest
Store PII in the partition key for uniqueness
Log all items for debugging
questions.explain: Default encryption at rest protects the underlying storage but any principal with table read access still sees plaintext, so genuinely sensitive attributes warrant client-side encryption plus tight IAM scoping. Putting PII in a partition key exposes it in keys, indexes and logs, and logging items broadcasts the data to anyone with log access.

questions.scenario: An application must allow a user to download only their own file from S3, with a link valid for 15 minutes. What is the correct implementation?
options: Server-side, verify the user owns the object and generate a 15-minute presigned URL for that specific key
Return a list of all object keys and let the client choose
Make the bucket public with obscure key names
Give the client IAM credentials
questions.explain: Authorising server-side and then issuing a short-lived presigned URL for exactly that key means the client never receives credentials and cannot reach other users' objects. Returning all keys leaks information, obscure names in a public bucket is security through obscurity, and handing IAM credentials to a client is a serious exposure.

questions.scenario: Which statement about IAM policy evaluation with a resource-based policy and a permission boundary is correct?
options: The request is allowed only if it passes the identity policy or resource policy, the permission boundary, and any service control policy, with no explicit deny anywhere
Only the resource policy matters
Permission boundaries grant access directly
Explicit deny can be overridden by a resource policy
questions.explain: Every applicable policy type must permit the action — identity or resource policy, permission boundary and any SCP — and a single explicit deny anywhere is final. Boundaries and SCPs cap permissions without ever granting them, and no policy type can override an explicit deny.

questions.scenario: A team must reduce CodeBuild costs for a pipeline running 500 builds per day. Which change is MOST effective?
options: Enable dependency caching and choose the smallest compute type that meets the build's needs
Always use the largest compute type
Disable all tests
Run builds on a schedule instead of on commit
questions.explain: CodeBuild bills per build minute by compute type, so caching dependencies shortens builds and right-sizing compute lowers the rate — together cutting cost without weakening the pipeline. The largest compute type raises the rate, disabling tests trades correctness for cost, and scheduled builds delay feedback while still incurring build minutes.

questions.scenario: Which CloudFormation practice reduces the risk and cost of a failed production deployment MOST?
options: Deploy to a staging stack from the same template first, then review a production change set before executing
Deploy directly to production and fix forward
Skip change sets to save time
Use different templates per environment
questions.explain: Exercising the same template in staging catches template errors before production, and the change set then reveals exactly what will be added, modified or replaced. Deploying straight to production discovers problems with real users, skipping change sets removes the preview, and divergent templates mean staging no longer proves anything.

questions.scenario: A team wants to reduce the blast radius of deployments across 40 microservices. Which approach is BEST?
options: Independent pipelines and stacks per service, deployed with canary or blue/green strategies
One pipeline deploying all 40 simultaneously
Manual deployment of all services together
One CloudFormation stack containing all 40
questions.explain: Independent pipelines and stacks mean a failure affects one service rather than forty, and gradual rollout limits exposure further. Deploying everything at once — whether by pipeline, by hand, or in a single stack — couples all services into one failure domain and makes rollback all-or-nothing.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST cost-effective way to run integration tests that need a database, in a pipeline running 50 times per day?
options: Spin up an ephemeral test environment per run and tear it down afterwards, or use a shared small test instance
Run tests against production
Maintain a permanently running production-sized test environment
Skip integration tests
questions.explain: Ephemeral environments exist only while the tests run, so cost tracks usage rather than uptime, and a small shared instance is a reasonable alternative for lighter needs. Testing against production risks data corruption and outages, a permanent production-sized environment is idle most of the day, and skipping tests removes the safety net.

questions.scenario: An ECS service on Fargate runs 10 tasks continuously at 20 percent CPU utilisation. What is the MOST effective cost optimisation?
options: Right-size the task CPU and memory to actual usage, and use service auto scaling to match demand
Increase the task size
Add more tasks
Switch to EC2 launch type without changing sizing
questions.explain: Fargate bills for the CPU and memory reserved rather than used, so 20 percent utilisation means paying roughly five times what the workload needs. Right-sizing plus auto scaling aligns cost with demand. Larger or more tasks increase spend, and changing launch type without resizing keeps the same over-provisioning while adding server management.

questions.scenario: Which practice MOST reduces the time to recover from a bad deployment?
options: Keeping the previous version deployable and rollback automated, for example via aliases or task definition revisions
Investigating fully before taking any action
Rebuilding from source during the incident
Waiting for the next scheduled release
questions.explain: An automated rollback to an artifact that already exists restores service in seconds, and investigation can follow once users are safe. Investigating first, rebuilding under pressure, or waiting for a scheduled release all extend the outage unnecessarily.

questions.scenario: Which TWO reduce the cost of a development environment that is only used during working hours?
options: Schedule non-production resources to stop outside working hours
Use serverless services that cost nothing when idle
Provision the same capacity as production
Run all environments continuously for convenience
Enable Multi-AZ on development databases
questions.explain: Stopping instances outside working hours can remove roughly two thirds of runtime cost, and serverless components charge nothing while idle. Matching production capacity, running continuously and enabling Multi-AZ all add cost for availability guarantees a development environment does not need.

questions.scenario: A CloudFormation stack takes 45 minutes to deploy because resources are created sequentially. What is the MOST effective improvement?
options: Remove unnecessary DependsOn attributes so independent resources are created in parallel
Increase the stack timeout
Deploy at night
Add more parameters
questions.explain: CloudFormation parallelises resource creation automatically except where dependencies exist, so unnecessary DependsOn attributes serialise work that could run concurrently. Timeouts, deployment timing and parameters do not change creation order or duration.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST balances deployment safety and speed for a service with 1,000 requests per second?
options: Canary deployment with automated alarm-based rollback
Manual approval before every deployment with no automated checks
All-at-once deployment with manual verification
Deploying only once per quarter
questions.explain: At that traffic level a canary exposes a small percentage of users while alarms decide automatically within minutes, giving both safety and speed. Manual gates without automated checks depend on a human noticing, all-at-once exposes everyone immediately, and quarterly releases make each change larger and riskier.

questions.scenario: Which is true about ECR image storage costs?
options: Storage is billed per gigabyte per month, so lifecycle policies removing untagged and old images reduce cost
Image storage is free
Only pulls are billed
Images are deleted automatically after 30 days
questions.explain: ECR bills for stored image data, and a repository accumulating every build artifact grows steadily. Lifecycle policies that expire untagged images and cap retained versions control this automatically. Images are never removed by default, and both storage and data transfer contribute to cost.

questions.scenario: A team must deploy the same infrastructure to development, staging and production with different sizing. What is the MOST maintainable approach?
options: One template with parameters or mappings controlling sizing per environment
Three separate templates
Manual resizing after each deployment
Identical sizing everywhere
questions.explain: A single parameterised template keeps one reviewed source of truth while allowing per-environment sizing, so a change applies everywhere consistently. Separate templates drift apart, manual resizing is forgotten and undone by the next deployment, and identical sizing either overspends in development or under-provisions production.

questions.scenario: Which statement about Lambda provisioned concurrency cost is correct?
options: You pay for provisioned capacity whether or not it is used, so it suits predictable traffic rather than sporadic workloads
It is free
It reduces cost for all workloads
It only bills during invocations
questions.explain: Provisioned concurrency charges for keeping environments warm regardless of traffic, which is worthwhile when latency matters and traffic is predictable, and wasteful for sporadic workloads. It reduces cold starts rather than cost, and billing continues during idle periods.

questions.scenario: Which practice reduces the risk that a pipeline deploys an untested dependency change?
options: Commit lockfiles and fail the build on unexpected dependency drift or known vulnerabilities
Always install the latest versions at build time
Ignore dependency updates
Update all dependencies manually in production
questions.explain: Lockfiles pin exact versions so builds are reproducible, and failing on drift or known vulnerabilities catches unexpected changes before deployment. Installing latest at build time means the artifact differs from what was tested, ignoring updates accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities, and manual production changes bypass all testing.

questions.scenario: A team must ensure that a rollback is possible even if the container registry loses the previous image tag. What practice helps MOST?
options: Use immutable tags and lifecycle policies that retain a defined number of recent images
Always overwrite the latest tag
Delete old images immediately after deployment
Store images only on developer machines
questions.explain: Immutable tags guarantee a given reference always resolves to the same image, and retention policies keep enough recent versions to roll back to. Overwriting a shared tag destroys the previous artifact, deleting images immediately removes the rollback target, and local-only storage is not available to the deployment platform.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST effective way to shorten a 20-minute pipeline that spends 15 minutes running tests?
options: Parallelise the test suite and run only affected tests where safe, keeping a full run before production
Delete half the tests
Increase the CodeBuild timeout
Run tests after deployment
questions.explain: Parallel execution reduces wall-clock time without reducing coverage, and selective testing on early stages with a full run before production balances speed and confidence. Deleting tests removes coverage permanently, timeouts do not speed anything up, and testing after deployment exposes users to defects.

questions.scenario: An application's CloudWatch bill is dominated by custom metrics. There are 50,000 unique metric combinations because a user ID is used as a dimension. What is the correct fix?
options: Remove high-cardinality dimensions such as user ID; keep them in logs and query with Logs Insights instead
Increase the metric resolution
Add more dimensions
Delete all metrics
questions.explain: CloudWatch bills per unique metric, and each distinct dimension value creates a separate metric, so a user ID dimension generates one per user. High-cardinality attributes belong in structured logs where they can be queried on demand. Higher resolution and extra dimensions increase cost further, and deleting all metrics removes monitoring.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST cost-effective way to keep 90 days of detailed request logs searchable while retaining 2 years for compliance?
options: 90 days in CloudWatch Logs, with older data exported to S3 and transitioned through cheaper storage classes
2 years entirely in CloudWatch Logs
90 days only, deleting the rest
Everything in DynamoDB
questions.explain: Recent logs stay in CloudWatch for interactive querying while older data moves to far cheaper S3 storage, satisfying both requirements at a fraction of the cost. Two years of CloudWatch retention is expensive, deleting breaks compliance, and DynamoDB is an unsuitable and costly log archive.

questions.scenario: A team must decide whether to enable detailed monitoring on 500 EC2 instances. What is the trade-off?
options: One-minute granularity aids faster detection but is charged per instance, so it suits critical instances rather than all 500
It is free and should always be enabled
It reduces cost
It has no effect on granularity
questions.explain: Detailed monitoring provides one-minute metrics instead of five-minute, which shortens detection time but carries a per-instance charge that becomes significant across a large fleet. Enabling it selectively on critical instances balances visibility and cost.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST reduces the cost of investigating rare errors in a high-volume application?
options: Log at a low level normally but capture full context for error paths, and sample traces with a higher rate for errors
Log everything at debug level
Log nothing and rely on user reports
Trace 100 percent of requests
questions.explain: Detailed capture only where it matters keeps ingestion and trace costs low while preserving the diagnostic detail needed for the rare failures. Debug logging everything and tracing every request are both prohibitively expensive at high volume, and relying on user reports means most errors are never seen.

questions.scenario: An application's p99 latency improved after enabling provisioned concurrency, but costs rose sharply. What analysis should guide the decision?
options: Compare the business value of the latency improvement against the provisioned capacity cost, and consider provisioning only for predictable peak periods
Always keep provisioned concurrency at maximum
Disable it regardless of the latency benefit
Increase memory instead
questions.explain: Provisioned concurrency is a deliberate cost-for-latency trade, so the right approach is to weigh the user-facing benefit against the spend and to schedule provisioning around known traffic patterns rather than running it continuously. Blanket maximum provisioning wastes money, and disabling it outright discards a real improvement.

questions.scenario: Which metric BEST indicates whether an ElastiCache cluster is correctly sized?
options: Cache hit rate together with eviction count and memory utilisation
Total request count only
The number of nodes
The cluster name
questions.explain: A falling hit rate alongside rising evictions and high memory utilisation shows the working set no longer fits and the cluster needs more memory. Request counts measure traffic rather than fit, and node count and naming are configuration details rather than health signals.

questions.scenario: A team discovers that 60 percent of Lambda cost comes from one function that runs on a schedule every minute but usually finds nothing to do. What is the BEST optimisation?
options: Replace polling with an event-driven trigger so the function runs only when there is work
Increase the schedule to every 10 minutes and accept the delay
Increase the function memory
Add provisioned concurrency
questions.explain: Polling pays for 1,440 invocations a day regardless of whether work exists, whereas an event-driven trigger such as an S3 notification, DynamoDB stream or EventBridge rule invokes only when something actually happens — removing the waste and reducing latency. Reducing frequency trades cost for delay, and memory and provisioned concurrency increase spend.

questions.scenario: Which is the MOST reliable indicator that a database index is missing for a frequently executed query?
options: High read capacity or CPU consumption relative to the number of rows actually returned
A high total request count
A large table size
A long table name
questions.explain: Reading far more data than is returned is the signature of a missing index — a Scan in DynamoDB or a full table scan in a relational database. Request volume and table size describe scale rather than efficiency, and naming is irrelevant.

questions.scenario: An application must reduce data transfer costs between services in the same region. Which change helps MOST?
options: Keep traffic within the same availability zone where possible and use VPC endpoints instead of NAT gateways for AWS service calls
Move services to different regions
Route all traffic through the public internet
Increase instance sizes
questions.explain: Cross-availability-zone traffic and NAT gateway data processing both carry per-gigabyte charges, so keeping traffic zone-local and using VPC endpoints for AWS service calls removes much of that cost. Cross-region traffic and public internet routing are more expensive, and instance sizing does not affect transfer pricing.

questions.scenario: Which practice MOST improves the signal-to-noise ratio of alerts?
options: Alert on user-facing symptoms with appropriate evaluation periods, rather than on every internal metric
Create an alarm for every available metric
Set all thresholds very low
Disable alerting entirely
questions.explain: Alerting on symptoms that matter to users, with evaluation periods that filter transient spikes, keeps pages meaningful and actionable. Alarming on every metric or setting thresholds very low produces noise that trains people to ignore alerts, and disabling alerting removes detection altogether.

questions.scenario: A team wants to know whether a caching change actually reduced database load. Which comparison is MOST direct?
options: Database read capacity or query count before and after, alongside the cache hit rate
Application log volume
The number of deployments
Instance uptime
questions.explain: Measuring database reads directly shows whether load fell, and the cache hit rate explains why. Log volume, deployment counts and uptime are unrelated to how much work the database is doing.

questions.scenario: Which approach BEST identifies the single most impactful performance improvement in a complex application?
options: Use X-Ray and profiling data to find the largest contributor to end-to-end latency, then optimise that first
Optimise the code that is easiest to change
Increase memory everywhere
Rewrite the application
questions.explain: Measuring where time is actually spent directs effort at the dominant bottleneck, which is where optimisation pays off most. Optimising whatever is convenient often improves something irrelevant, blanket memory increases raise cost without targeting the cause, and a rewrite is disproportionate and risky before the bottleneck is even known.
